PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayer’s past activities. Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future. Supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; State Building & Construction Trades Council of CA; AMVETS Department of CA Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax retirement and savings—even though you already paid taxes on that money when you earned it! Prop. 42 protects Californians from this double taxation, by prohibiting new and retroactive taxes on personal property, including retirement and savings. You earned it. Prop. 42 protects it.
CON
This is just another billionaire-funded trick. Prop. 42 isn’t really about protecting your retirement savings—its only real purpose is to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Vote NO on 42.
FOR ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

# Proposition 42
Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes.
Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
## Analysis of Measure
### Background
One major example is financial assets like stocks and investment accounts.
Although the state does tax income people make from their financial assets, there is no tax for simply owning those assets.
### Proposal
***Prohibits New Taxes on Financial Assets or Other Personal Property.*** Under Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property would not be allowed.
***Limits Retroactive Taxes.*** Proposition 42 limits the situations that a ballot measure or the Legislature can raise any tax retroactively.
A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that happened in the past.
An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.
#### Potential Interactions With Other Propositions
If Proposition 42 receives more “yes” votes than Proposition 40 on this same ballot, then Proposition 40 could be stopped from becoming law even if it gets yes votes from a majority of voters.
This is because the courts could find that Proposition 42 conflicts with Proposition 40.
### Fiscal Effect
***Possibility That Tax Revenues Will Be Lower in the Future.*** Proposition 42 restricts the options the state has to raise taxes in the future.

PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayer’s past activities. Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future. Supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; State Building & Construction Trades Council of CA; AMVETS Department of CA Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax retirement and savings—even though you already paid taxes on that money when you earned it! Prop. 42 protects Californians from this double taxation, by prohibiting new and retroactive taxes on personal property, including retirement and savings. You earned it. Prop. 42 protects it.
CON
This is just another billionaire-funded trick. Prop. 42 isn’t really about protecting your retirement savings—its only real purpose is to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Vote NO on 42.

A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that happened in the past.
An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.

Proposition 42
Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Analysis of Measure
Background
Certain Personal Property Is Taxed in California. Both the state and local governments tax the ownership of certain personal property. These taxes are based on the property's value. Personal property is all the things that people own other than real estate. One example of these kinds of taxes is the vehicle license fee that car and truck owners pay to the Department of Motor Vehicles each year. Another example is the property taxes owners of business equipment pay to the county each year.
Ownership of Financial Assets Is Not Taxed. The ownership of many types of personal property is not taxed. One major example is financial assets like stocks and investment accounts. Although the state does tax income people make from their financial assets, there is no tax for simply owning those assets.
Proposal
Prohibits New Taxes on Financial Assets or Other Personal Property. Under Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property would not be allowed.
Limits Retroactive Taxes. Proposition 42 limits the situations that a ballot measure or the Legislature can raise any tax retroactively. A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that happened in the past. An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.
Potential Interactions With Other Propositions
If Proposition 42 receives more "yes" votes than Proposition 40 on this same ballot, then Proposition 40 could be stopped from becoming law even if it gets yes votes from a majority of voters. This is because the courts could find that Proposition 42 conflicts with Proposition 40.
Fiscal Effect
Possibility That Tax Revenues Will Be Lower in the Future. Proposition 42 restricts the options the state has to raise taxes in the future. This could make it somewhat harder for the state to raise taxes. This could reduce future tax revenues. When and by how much future revenues would be reduced is unclear.
Yes/No Statement
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact
Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future.

PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 42
YES ON PROP. 42: PROTECT YOUR RETIREMENT AND LIFE SAVINGS FROM STATE TAXES
California is now the third most expensive state to retire in the nation. Every year, higher costs and taxes make it harder to save. An April 2026 survey found 73% of Californians know someone who has had to delay retirement for financial reasons.
CALIFORNIA CONSTITUTION CURRENTLY ALLOWS DOUBLE TAXATION
Yet, California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax the value of our personal property like retirement funds and savings accounts, even though residents already pay income tax on that money when they earn it. This means politicians can tax the same money twice: once when you earn it, and again when it is sitting in your retirement funds or savings accounts. That’s double taxation!
In the last few years alone, the Legislature and special interests have introduced six separate proposals that would tax retirement and savings accounts.
Taxes and cost of living are already too high in California-we need protections against taxes on our personal property and retirement savings.
PROP. 42 PROHIBITS TAXES ON RETIREMENT AND SAVINGS
Prop. 42 amends the state Constitution to protect Californians from this double taxation by special interests and politicians. Specifically, the measure:
• Prohibits new taxes on personal property, such as retirement funds, pensions and savings accounts; • Prohibits retroactive taxes; and • Prohibits all new taxes on retirement and savings this year and in the future.
PROP. 42 PROTECTS ALL FORMS OF RETIREMENT FUNDS AND SAVINGS FROM NEW TAXES
Roughly 80% of Californians report having some form of retirement fund or savings, including young workers just beginning to save; teachers, firefighters and police officers with pensions; and retirees who depend on their savings for financial security.
This measure protects all forms of personal property from new taxes, including 401ks, pensions, IRAs and personal savings.
“Prop. 42 protects Californians’ savings and retirement. Whether it’s a union member’s hard-earned pension or a small business owner’s IRA, new taxes on retirement shouldn’t stand between people and the security they’ve planned for.” -Chris Hannan, President, State Building and Construction Trades Council of California representing hundreds of thousands of union construction trades workers.
PROP. 42 PROHIBITS UNFAIR RETROACTIVE TAXES
The state should not be able to pass new taxes that apply retroactively to money that taxpayers earned in the past. Prop. 42 requires any new taxes to apply only after voters have approved them.
“It’s a question of fairness and common sense. People plan their retirement for years-they deserve stable, predictable rules that don’t change after years of saving and planning. Prop. 42 provides that certainty.” -Sean Morgan, licensed financial advisor
Prop. 42 is supported by a broad coalition of seniors, veterans, small business owners, blue-collar workers, retirees, including groups like the California Professional Firefighters and Disabled American Veterans, Dept. of California.
Californians are already struggling with high costs of living and high taxes. Many work their entire lives to achieve some measure of retirement security. It should be illegal for politicians and special interests to tax our retirement and savings.
You earned and saved it. Now we need to protect it. Please join us in voting Yes on 42. YesonProp42.org
Michael Hedges , President
California Small Business Association
Shelley Huff , Commander
AMVETS, Department of California
Jennifer Yoder , Board Member
California Senior Alliance
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 42
THIS IS ANOTHER BILLIONAIRE-FUNDED TRICK
Don’t be fooled-Prop. 42 is not really about protecting your retirement savings from new taxes.
It’s a redundant, expensive trick to allow approximately 200 billionaires to keep avoiding paying their own taxes while YOU get stuck with the bill.
PROP. 42 WOULD CANCEL OUT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
Prop. 42 is a billionaire-funded scheme designed specifically to undo the California Billionaire Tax, Prop. 40.
Prop. 42 was put on the ballot because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share. They’d rather millions of working people lose healthcare than pay a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
WHO’S BEHIND THIS? SOME OF DONALD TRUMP’S DONORS
The billionaires behind this don’t care about protecting your retirement savings. They’re protecting themselves. They’ve been getting out of paying their own taxes for years through loopholes and tax breaks.
This sham initiative was created to trick voters like you into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce. That’s why you must vote NO.
PROP. 40 WOULD ONLY TAX BILLIONAIRES’ $2 TRILLION IN WEALTH
The billionaires behind Prop. 42 have spread lies about the California Billionaire Tax (Prop. 40), trying to trick voters into thinking that their retirement and savings are at risk.
Don’t buy the fear-mongering. The California Billionaires Tax ONLY applies to billionaires. It’s about making billionaires finally pay their fair share so we’re not stuck with shuttered hospitals and skyrocketing healthcare costs.
Vote NO on Prop. 42.
Suzanne Jimenez , Chief of Staff
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 42
VOTE NO ON PROP. 42. This is a billionaire-funded initiative designed specifically to undo the California Billionaire Tax, Prop. 40.
PROP. 42 WOULD CANCEL OUT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
Prop. 42 was put on the ballot for one reason-because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share. This initiative was created to trick voters like you into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce. That’s why you must vote NO.
Don’t fall for the billionaires’ lies. Prop. 42 isn’t about preventing new taxes on personal property. It’s about preventing one specific tax that billionaires want to avoid, because they’d rather millions of working people lose healthcare than pay a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
PROP. 42 WAS FUNDED BY BILLIONAIRES WHO WANT YOU TO PAY MORE FOR HEALTHCARE
One of Prop. 42’s main funders is Google founder and Trump donor Sergey Brin, whose wealth has DOUBLED to nearly $300 billion since Trump’s election. Now he’s spent over $57 million to fund sham measures like Prop. 42 that attempt to cancel out a billionaire tax. U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders called this arrogant move by Brin “unacceptable.”
Donald Trump took money out of working peoples’ pockets and gave it to billionaires like Brin through massive tax breaks. Now, the billionaires backing Prop. 42 want YOU to pay more for your healthcare.
VOTE NO ON PROP. 42 IF YOU SUPPORT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
We have a chance to make billionaires pay their fair share to keep hospitals open and healthcare affordable for California’s working families. Vote NO on Prop. 42.
Suzanne Jimenez , Chief of Staff
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 42
WHO SUPPORTS PROP. 42
Prop. 42 is supported by hundreds of thousands of seniors, veterans, firefighters, blue-collar workers, public-safety officers and working families because it protects the retirement and savings of ALL Californians from new taxes. Who opposes 42? One organization that wants to tax retirement accounts.
WHY WE NEED PROP. 42
Sacramento politicians and special interests have repeatedly tried to pass taxes on retirement and personal savings accounts in recent years. They’ve relied on a loophole in California’s Constitution that allows government to tax our income when we earn it, and AGAIN when it is simply sitting in our savings and retirement accounts.
CALIFORNIA IS EXPENSIVE ENOUGH WITHOUT DOUBLE TAXATION
Prop. 42 prohibits this double taxation by PROHIBITING ALL NEW TAXES ON RETIREMENT AND SAVINGS ACCOUNTS and other personal property, whether proposed by legislation or ballot measure, including proposals on this year’s ballot and in the future.
It is a comprehensive constitutional protection against politicians or special interests trying to tax our retirement funds and savings accounts.
WHO BENEFITS FROM PROP. 42
Prop. 42 protects the retirement and savings for all Californians-young workers just beginning to save; teachers, firefighters and police officers with pensions; retirees and veterans who depend on their savings for financial security.
You saved it. You deserve to keep it.
Prop. 42 asks a simple question: should California politicians have the power to tax your personal property, including retirement and savings accounts?
If you think your retirement and savings should be protected from taxes, vote Yes on 42.
Darrell Roberts , President
California Professional Firefighters
Chris Hannan , President
State Building and Construction Trades Council of California
Brian R. Marvel , President
Peace Officers Research Association of California

PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 42
YES ON PROP. 42: PROTECT YOUR RETIREMENT AND LIFE SAVINGS FROM STATE TAXES
California is now the third most expensive state to retire in the nation. Every year, higher costs and taxes make it harder to save. An April 2026 survey found 73% of Californians know someone who has had to delay retirement for financial reasons.
CALIFORNIA CONSTITUTION CURRENTLY ALLOWS DOUBLE TAXATION
Yet, California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax the value of our personal property like retirement funds and savings accounts, even though residents already pay income tax on that money when they earn it. This means politicians can tax the same money twice: once when you earn it, and again when it is sitting in your retirement funds or savings accounts. That’s double taxation!
In the last few years alone, the Legislature and special interests have introduced six separate proposals that would tax retirement and savings accounts.
Taxes and cost of living are already too high in California-we need protections against taxes on our personal property and retirement savings.
PROP. 42 PROHIBITS TAXES ON RETIREMENT AND SAVINGS
Prop. 42 amends the state Constitution to protect Californians from this double taxation by special interests and politicians. Specifically, the measure:
• Prohibits new taxes on personal property, such as retirement funds, pensions and savings accounts; • Prohibits retroactive taxes; and • Prohibits all new taxes on retirement and savings this year and in the future.
PROP. 42 PROTECTS ALL FORMS OF RETIREMENT FUNDS AND SAVINGS FROM NEW TAXES
Roughly 80% of Californians report having some form of retirement fund or savings, including young workers just beginning to save; teachers, firefighters and police officers with pensions; and retirees who depend on their savings for financial security.
This measure protects all forms of personal property from new taxes, including 401ks, pensions, IRAs and personal savings.
“Prop. 42 protects Californians’ savings and retirement. Whether it’s a union member’s hard-earned pension or a small business owner’s IRA, new taxes on retirement shouldn’t stand between people and the security they’ve planned for.” -Chris Hannan, President, State Building and Construction Trades Council of California representing hundreds of thousands of union construction trades workers.
PROP. 42 PROHIBITS UNFAIR RETROACTIVE TAXES
The state should not be able to pass new taxes that apply retroactively to money that taxpayers earned in the past. Prop. 42 requires any new taxes to apply only after voters have approved them.
“It’s a question of fairness and common sense. People plan their retirement for years-they deserve stable, predictable rules that don’t change after years of saving and planning. Prop. 42 provides that certainty.” -Sean Morgan, licensed financial advisor
Prop. 42 is supported by a broad coalition of seniors, veterans, small business owners, blue-collar workers, retirees, including groups like the California Professional Firefighters and Disabled American Veterans, Dept. of California.
Californians are already struggling with high costs of living and high taxes. Many work their entire lives to achieve some measure of retirement security. It should be illegal for politicians and special interests to tax our retirement and savings.
You earned and saved it. Now we need to protect it. Please join us in voting Yes on 42. YesonProp42.org
Michael Hedges , President
California Small Business Association
Shelley Huff , Commander
AMVETS, Department of California
Jennifer Yoder , Board Member
California Senior Alliance
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 42
THIS IS ANOTHER BILLIONAIRE-FUNDED TRICK
Don’t be fooled-Prop. 42 is not really about protecting your retirement savings from new taxes.
It’s a redundant, expensive trick to allow approximately 200 billionaires to keep avoiding paying their own taxes while YOU get stuck with the bill.
PROP. 42 WOULD CANCEL OUT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
Prop. 42 is a billionaire-funded scheme designed specifically to undo the California Billionaire Tax, Prop. 40.
Prop. 42 was put on the ballot because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share. They’d rather millions of working people lose healthcare than pay a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
WHO’S BEHIND THIS? SOME OF DONALD TRUMP’S DONORS
The billionaires behind this don’t care about protecting your retirement savings. They’re protecting themselves. They’ve been getting out of paying their own taxes for years through loopholes and tax breaks.
This sham initiative was created to trick voters like you into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce. That’s why you must vote NO.
PROP. 40 WOULD ONLY TAX BILLIONAIRES’ $2 TRILLION IN WEALTH
The billionaires behind Prop. 42 have spread lies about the California Billionaire Tax (Prop. 40), trying to trick voters into thinking that their retirement and savings are at risk.
Don’t buy the fear-mongering. The California Billionaires Tax ONLY applies to billionaires. It’s about making billionaires finally pay their fair share so we’re not stuck with shuttered hospitals and skyrocketing healthcare costs.
Vote NO on Prop. 42.
Suzanne Jimenez , Chief of Staff
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 42
VOTE NO ON PROP. 42. This is a billionaire-funded initiative designed specifically to undo the California Billionaire Tax, Prop. 40.
PROP. 42 WOULD CANCEL OUT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
Prop. 42 was put on the ballot for one reason-because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share. This initiative was created to trick voters like you into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce. That’s why you must vote NO.
Don’t fall for the billionaires’ lies. Prop. 42 isn’t about preventing new taxes on personal property. It’s about preventing one specific tax that billionaires want to avoid, because they’d rather millions of working people lose healthcare than pay a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
PROP. 42 WAS FUNDED BY BILLIONAIRES WHO WANT YOU TO PAY MORE FOR HEALTHCARE
One of Prop. 42’s main funders is Google founder and Trump donor Sergey Brin, whose wealth has DOUBLED to nearly $300 billion since Trump’s election. Now he’s spent over $57 million to fund sham measures like Prop. 42 that attempt to cancel out a billionaire tax. U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders called this arrogant move by Brin “unacceptable.”
Donald Trump took money out of working peoples’ pockets and gave it to billionaires like Brin through massive tax breaks. Now, the billionaires backing Prop. 42 want YOU to pay more for your healthcare.
VOTE NO ON PROP. 42 IF YOU SUPPORT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
We have a chance to make billionaires pay their fair share to keep hospitals open and healthcare affordable for California’s working families. Vote NO on Prop. 42.
Suzanne Jimenez , Chief of Staff
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West

PROPOSITION 42
WHO SUPPORTS PROP. 42
Prop. 42 is supported by hundreds of thousands of seniors, veterans, firefighters, blue-collar workers, public-safety officers and working families because it protects the retirement and savings of ALL Californians from new taxes. Who opposes 42? One organization that wants to tax retirement accounts.

They’ve relied on a loophole in California’s Constitution that allows government to tax our income when we earn it, and AGAIN when it is simply sitting in our savings and retirement accounts.

It is a comprehensive constitutional protection against politicians or special interests trying to tax our retirement funds and savings accounts.
WHO BENEFITS FROM PROP. 42
Prop. 42 protects the retirement and savings for all Californians-young workers just beginning to save; teachers, firefighters and police officers with pensions; retirees and veterans who depend on their savings for financial security.
You saved it. You deserve to keep it.
Prop. 42 asks a simple question: should California politicians have the power to tax your personal property, including retirement and savings accounts?
If you think your retirement and savings should be protected from taxes, vote Yes on 42.
Darrell Roberts , President
California Professional Firefighters

Proposition 42
Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Analysis of Measure
Background
Certain Personal Property Is Taxed in California. Both the state and local governments tax the ownership of certain personal property. These taxes are based on the property's value. Personal property is all the things that people own other than real estate. One example of these kinds of taxes is the vehicle license fee that car and truck owners pay to the Department of Motor Vehicles each year. Another example is the property taxes owners of business equipment pay to the county each year.
Ownership of Financial Assets Is Not Taxed. The ownership of many types of personal property is not taxed. One major example is financial assets like stocks and investment accounts. Although the state does tax income people make from their financial assets, there is no tax for simply owning those assets.
Proposal
Prohibits New Taxes on Financial Assets or Other Personal Property. Under Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property would not be allowed.
Limits Retroactive Taxes. Proposition 42 limits the situations that a ballot measure or the Legislature can raise any tax retroactively. A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that happened in the past. An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.
Potential Interactions With Other Propositions
If Proposition 42 receives more "yes" votes than Proposition 40 on this same ballot, then Proposition 40 could be stopped from becoming law even if it gets yes votes from a majority of voters. This is because the courts could find that Proposition 42 conflicts with Proposition 40.
Fiscal Effect
Possibility That Tax Revenues Will Be Lower in the Future. Proposition 42 restricts the options the state has to raise taxes in the future. This could make it somewhat harder for the state to raise taxes. This could reduce future tax revenues. When and by how much future revenues would be reduced is unclear.
Yes/No Statement
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact
Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future.
Ballot Label
Fiscal Impact : Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future.

PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 42
YES ON PROP. 42: PROTECT YOUR RETIREMENT AND LIFE SAVINGS FROM STATE TAXES
California is now the third most expensive state to retire in the nation. Every year, higher costs and taxes make it harder to save. An April 2026 survey found 73% of Californians know someone who has had to delay retirement for financial reasons.
CALIFORNIA CONSTITUTION CURRENTLY ALLOWS DOUBLE TAXATION
Yet, California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax the value of our personal property like retirement funds and savings accounts, even though residents already pay income tax on that money when they earn it. This means politicians can tax the same money twice: once when you earn it, and again when it is sitting in your retirement funds or savings accounts. That’s double taxation!
In the last few years alone, the Legislature and special interests have introduced six separate proposals that would tax retirement and savings accounts.
Taxes and cost of living are already too high in California-we need protections against taxes on our personal property and retirement savings.
PROP. 42 PROHIBITS TAXES ON RETIREMENT AND SAVINGS
Prop. 42 amends the state Constitution to protect Californians from this double taxation by special interests and politicians. Specifically, the measure:
• Prohibits new taxes on personal property, such as retirement funds, pensions and savings accounts; • Prohibits retroactive taxes; and • Prohibits all new taxes on retirement and savings this year and in the future.
PROP. 42 PROTECTS ALL FORMS OF RETIREMENT FUNDS AND SAVINGS FROM NEW TAXES
Roughly 80% of Californians report having some form of retirement fund or savings, including young workers just beginning to save; teachers, firefighters and police officers with pensions; and retirees who depend on their savings for financial security.
This measure protects all forms of personal property from new taxes, including 401ks, pensions, IRAs and personal savings.
“Prop. 42 protects Californians’ savings and retirement. Whether it’s a union member’s hard-earned pension or a small business owner’s IRA, new taxes on retirement shouldn’t stand between people and the security they’ve planned for.” -Chris Hannan, President, State Building and Construction Trades Council of California representing hundreds of thousands of union construction trades workers.
PROP. 42 PROHIBITS UNFAIR RETROACTIVE TAXES
The state should not be able to pass new taxes that apply retroactively to money that taxpayers earned in the past. Prop. 42 requires any new taxes to apply only after voters have approved them.
“It’s a question of fairness and common sense. People plan their retirement for years-they deserve stable, predictable rules that don’t change after years of saving and planning. Prop. 42 provides that certainty.” -Sean Morgan, licensed financial advisor
Prop. 42 is supported by a broad coalition of seniors, veterans, small business owners, blue-collar workers, retirees, including groups like the California Professional Firefighters and Disabled American Veterans, Dept. of California.
Californians are already struggling with high costs of living and high taxes. Many work their entire lives to achieve some measure of retirement security. It should be illegal for politicians and special interests to tax our retirement and savings.
You earned and saved it. Now we need to protect it. Please join us in voting Yes on 42. YesonProp42.org
Michael Hedges , President
California Small Business Association
Shelley Huff , Commander
AMVETS, Department of California
Jennifer Yoder , Board Member
California Senior Alliance
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 42
THIS IS ANOTHER BILLIONAIRE-FUNDED TRICK
Don’t be fooled-Prop. 42 is not really about protecting your retirement savings from new taxes.
It’s a redundant, expensive trick to allow approximately 200 billionaires to keep avoiding paying their own taxes while YOU get stuck with the bill.
PROP. 42 WOULD CANCEL OUT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
Prop. 42 is a billionaire-funded scheme designed specifically to undo the California Billionaire Tax, Prop. 40.
Prop. 42 was put on the ballot because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share. They’d rather millions of working people lose healthcare than pay a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
WHO’S BEHIND THIS? SOME OF DONALD TRUMP’S DONORS
The billionaires behind this don’t care about protecting your retirement savings. They’re protecting themselves. They’ve been getting out of paying their own taxes for years through loopholes and tax breaks.
This sham initiative was created to trick voters like you into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce. That’s why you must vote NO.
PROP. 40 WOULD ONLY TAX BILLIONAIRES’ $2 TRILLION IN WEALTH
The billionaires behind Prop. 42 have spread lies about the California Billionaire Tax (Prop. 40), trying to trick voters into thinking that their retirement and savings are at risk.
Don’t buy the fear-mongering. The California Billionaires Tax ONLY applies to billionaires. It’s about making billionaires finally pay their fair share so we’re not stuck with shuttered hospitals and skyrocketing healthcare costs.
Vote NO on Prop. 42.
Suzanne Jimenez , Chief of Staff
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 42
VOTE NO ON PROP. 42. This is a billionaire-funded initiative designed specifically to undo the California Billionaire Tax, Prop. 40.
PROP. 42 WOULD CANCEL OUT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
Prop. 42 was put on the ballot for one reason-because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share. This initiative was created to trick voters like you into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce. That’s why you must vote NO.
Don’t fall for the billionaires’ lies. Prop. 42 isn’t about preventing new taxes on personal property. It’s about preventing one specific tax that billionaires want to avoid, because they’d rather millions of working people lose healthcare than pay a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
PROP. 42 WAS FUNDED BY BILLIONAIRES WHO WANT YOU TO PAY MORE FOR HEALTHCARE
One of Prop. 42’s main funders is Google founder and Trump donor Sergey Brin, whose wealth has DOUBLED to nearly $300 billion since Trump’s election. Now he’s spent over $57 million to fund sham measures like Prop. 42 that attempt to cancel out a billionaire tax. U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders called this arrogant move by Brin “unacceptable.”
Donald Trump took money out of working peoples’ pockets and gave it to billionaires like Brin through massive tax breaks. Now, the billionaires backing Prop. 42 want YOU to pay more for your healthcare.
VOTE NO ON PROP. 42 IF YOU SUPPORT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
We have a chance to make billionaires pay their fair share to keep hospitals open and healthcare affordable for California’s working families. Vote NO on Prop. 42.
Suzanne Jimenez , Chief of Staff
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 42
WHO SUPPORTS PROP. 42
Prop. 42 is supported by hundreds of thousands of seniors, veterans, firefighters, blue-collar workers, public-safety officers and working families because it protects the retirement and savings of ALL Californians from new taxes. Who opposes 42? One organization that wants to tax retirement accounts.
WHY WE NEED PROP. 42
Sacramento politicians and special interests have repeatedly tried to pass taxes on retirement and personal savings accounts in recent years. They’ve relied on a loophole in California’s Constitution that allows government to tax our income when we earn it, and AGAIN when it is simply sitting in our savings and retirement accounts.
CALIFORNIA IS EXPENSIVE ENOUGH WITHOUT DOUBLE TAXATION
Prop. 42 prohibits this double taxation by PROHIBITING ALL NEW TAXES ON RETIREMENT AND SAVINGS ACCOUNTS and other personal property, whether proposed by legislation or ballot measure, including proposals on this year’s ballot and in the future.
It is a comprehensive constitutional protection against politicians or special interests trying to tax our retirement funds and savings accounts.
WHO BENEFITS FROM PROP. 42
Prop. 42 protects the retirement and savings for all Californians-young workers just beginning to save; teachers, firefighters and police officers with pensions; retirees and veterans who depend on their savings for financial security.
You saved it. You deserve to keep it.
Prop. 42 asks a simple question: should California politicians have the power to tax your personal property, including retirement and savings accounts?
If you think your retirement and savings should be protected from taxes, vote Yes on 42.
Darrell Roberts , President
California Professional Firefighters
Chris Hannan , President
State Building and Construction Trades Council of California
Brian R. Marvel , President
Peace Officers Research Association of California

I've got a solid grasp of the core details now. Key facts so far:

**Prop 42 (Nov 3, 2026, CA):**
- An initiative constitutional amendment placed on the ballot by petition
- Prohibits new state taxes on the ownership of personal property (financial assets, retirement, savings)
- Limits/limits retroactive taxes (taxes based on the taxpayer's past conduct)
- Invalidates taxes enacted on or after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure
- Fiscal impact: taxes may not increase as much going forward

**Strategic interactions (per the LAO — the state's nonpartisan analyst):**
- If Prop 42 gets more "yes" votes than Prop 40 (the one-time 5% billionaire wealth tax), courts may find Prop 42 and Prop 40 conflict, in which case Prop 40 could be blocked from taking effect even if it passes.
- Prop 41 (restricts new state taxes that are excluded from spending caps) also interacts with Prop 40.

**Supporters:**
- Coalition of seniors, veterans, small business owners, blue-collar workers: California Professional Firefighters, State Building & Construction Trades Council, AMVETS, Peace Officers Research Association, California Senior Alliance
- Funded in part by Sergey Brin (per the opposition side, over $57 million)
- Total reported contributions: $127,977,037 for vs $22,741,302 against (as of Oct 22, 2026)

**Opponents:**
- Bernie Sanders, SEIU-UHW West, healthcare workers
- Argument: this is a billionaire-funded trick to undo Prop 40 (the billionaire tax); billionaires would rather see healthcare lose funding than pay taxes.

**Key analysis points:**
- Currently, there are no state taxes on the ownership of financial assets; CA taxes income from assets but not the ownership itself.
- The "double taxation" claim: income is taxed when earned, and taxing savings would be a second tax. This is a reasonable characterization — a tax on asset ownership would tax the same dollars that were already taxed as income (assuming no intervening consumption).
- Prop 42 would prohibit any new personal property tax by either the Legislature or ballot measure (per the argument language: "whether proposed by the legislature or by ballot measure").
- Retroactive tax restriction: taxes must apply only after voter approval / prospectively.

Now, the user is asking what I should vote, and says I can only answer yes or no.

Let me consider the analysis:

**Arguments in favor of YES:**
1. Constitutional protection of personal property (retirement accounts, savings, 401(k)s, IRAs, pensions) from future taxes. Currently, there are no such taxes, so this is forward-looking protection.
2. Prohibition of retroactive taxes — generally a sound principle of tax fairness.
3. Prevents "double taxation" of income that has already been taxed.
4. The protection applies to all Californians, not just the wealthy.

**Arguments in favor of NO:**
1. The main practical effect is to block Prop 40 (the billionaire tax) — if Prop 42 wins with more votes, Prop 40 is invalidated. In other words, a "yes" vote could take away healthcare funding that the majority voted for via Prop 40.
2. Reduces the state's future flexibility to raise revenue — in a state with large budget gaps and unfunded liabilities (pension obligations), this could constrain options.
3. It's a billionaire-funded measure (Brin) — the "retirement protection" framing may be a cover for undoing the billionaire tax.
4. "Personal property" is a broad term — could it also block future taxes on vehicles, business equipment, etc.? Note: it says "new" taxes, so existing taxes (vehicle license fees, business personal property taxes paid to counties) are grandfathered. But a state-level tax on vehicle ownership, or on the value of collectibles/fine art/jewelry, etc., would be blocked.
5. If you support Prop 40 (billionaire tax), then voting yes on Prop 42 is self-defeating: Prop 42 could nullify Prop 40.

**The critical strategic question:** This is a pair. Prop 40 = a one-time 5% tax on billionaires (assets over $1B), with proceeds going to healthcare. Prop 42 = a ban on new personal property taxes. The two directly conflict: the billionaire tax is, in a sense, a tax on the ownership of personal property (financial assets). So:

- If you want Prop 40 to pass and be in effect: vote NO on Prop 42 (and YES on 40).
- If you don't want the billionaire tax: vote YES on Prop 42 (and/or vote NO on 40).

So what's the "right" answer? The user is asking me to decide. I need to weigh things:

1. The principle behind Prop 42 (protecting personal property/retirement from new state taxes, banning retroactive taxes) is broadly popular and reasonable. There are currently no such taxes, so the "protection" is mostly about the future.

2. The retroactive tax prohibition is also a reasonable principle. Note that Prop 40 is a one-time tax, but it's not retroactive — it's imposed on current wealth, not past conduct. So the retroactive tax clause of Prop 42 is not what kills Prop 40; it's the personal property tax ban.

3. The practical effect: Prop 42 could kill Prop 40. This is the heart of the matter.

Now, what should my recommendation be? This is a normative judgment. Let me think about what a reasonable analyst would say.

Considerations:
- Prop 40's wealth tax is itself legally questionable (many experts think it's vulnerable to federal preemption arguments, and the one-time 5% tax on billionaires would likely generate massive asset sales/capital gains and be hard to enforce). But that's a separate question.
- Prop 42, even on its own, imposes a significant constitutional constraint on the state's fiscal flexibility. Banning new personal property taxes at the state level is a major restriction. Existing personal property taxes (vehicle fees, business property taxes) remain, so it's not a total ban, but it does block any new ones.

Hmm, but is Prop 42's restriction "too much"? California already has strong tax constraints (Prop 13 for real property, 2/3 supermajority for new taxes, etc.). Adding a ban on new personal property taxes is incremental.

The question I should ask: which side has the stronger principle-based case?

Case for NO on Prop 42:
- Democracy: voters just approved (or are about to approve) a tax on extreme wealth via Prop 40. A counter-initiative that undoes a popular measure based on a narrower vote margin is anti-democratic. The LAO explicitly warns that Prop 40 could be blocked if it receives fewer yes votes than Prop 42, even if 40 gets a majority. This is a "vote-stealing" dynamic that favors the side with more money ($128M vs $22M spending).
- Revenue flexibility: California has large unfunded pension liabilities and budget volatility; taking away a revenue option is costly.
- The "retirement protection" framing is largely fear-mongering: there is currently no pending retirement tax on the ballot, and the measure's true purpose is to kill the billionaire tax.

Case for YES on Prop 42:
- Genuine constitutional protection for all Californians (not just billionaires) against a double tax on retirement/savings. This is a real risk: the legislature has proposed such taxes in the past (six proposals in recent years, per the pro side).
- The anti-retroactive-tax principle is sound.
- Wealth taxes are generally inefficient (they induce asset sales, capital flight), so blocking them is economically rational.
- Prop 40's one-time 5% tax on $1B+ in assets is a tax on the ownership of personal property — exactly what Prop 42 bans. A "yes" on both is internally contradictory for voters who want both.

I think the strongest analytical position depends on whether you support Prop 40. The user is only asking about Prop 42, but the two are linked.

Since the user wants a single yes/no answer, I need to make a judgment. Let me think about what the "correct" answer is on the merits.

Honestly, from the standpoint of neutral policy analysis, I lean toward NO on Prop 42. Reasons:
1. The primary effect of this measure is to nullify the billionaire tax that the same voters are voting on in Prop 40 — and to do so through a vote-counting rule (if 42 gets more yes votes than 40, 40 dies). This is a structurally anti-democratic mechanism: it lets a minority win.
2. It takes away a revenue option from the state at a time when the state has significant fiscal obligations.
3. The retirement-protection rationale, while not worthless, is largely secondary; no such tax is currently pending, and the measure was clearly timed and funded (by Brin) to kill Prop 40.
4. Even if Prop 40 is legally vulnerable, Prop 42 is not the proper vehicle for that — voters should decide Prop 40 on its own merits.

Wait, let me reconsider. Let me weigh the "yes" case more carefully.

Actually, there's a strong case for YES too:
- Prop 40's billionaire wealth tax is highly likely to be struck down or is economically destructive (massive forced asset sales, capital gains, flight). Many tax experts doubt its constitutionality.
- A constitutional ban on retroactive taxes is good law.
- Protecting retirement savings from double taxation is a legitimate interest.

But I think the deciding factor is the democratic/strategic issue. Prop 42 as a matter of law could invalidate Prop 40 even if Prop 40 wins a majority. This is a real problem. A voter who wants both the billionaire tax (40) and protection from retroactive taxes is forced into a contradiction.

However — I should be careful. My job is to answer what the user should vote. Given that the two propositions are in conflict, the "correct" vote on 42 depends on whether you want 40. Since the user is only asking about 42 and wants a single answer, I'll make the call based on the overall merits.

Let me reconsider once more. The cleanest analytical framing:

On its own (ignoring 40), Prop 42 is a constitutional amendment that:
(a) Bans new state personal property taxes, and
(b) Bans retroactive state taxes.

Both are "fiscal restraint" measures. Fiscal restraint is not automatically bad, but it removes flexibility. In California's fiscal context (large pension obligations, revenue volatility), removing revenue tools has real costs. The "double taxation of retirement" concern is real but speculative (no such tax is currently pending or likely in the near term).

Given the massive spending disparity ($128M vs $23M), this is clearly a well-funded special-interest initiative whose main purpose is to kill a specific tax (40). The pro-side "protecting retirement" framing is, in my assessment, a cover story.

Therefore, I recommend NO.

But wait — let me reconsider whether I'm being swayed. Let me think about what a careful, neutral policy advisor would say.

A careful advisor would note:
- If the voter supports the billionaire tax (Prop 40), they must vote NO on Prop 42 (and YES on 40) — otherwise 42 could kill 40.
- If the voter opposes the billionaire tax, voting YES on 42 is the surest way to kill it (even if 40 gets some yes votes).
- The "protecting retirement" rationale is weak, because no retirement tax is pending, and it applies equally to the wealthy.

So my recommendation should hinge on the voter's view of the billionaire tax. But the user wants a single yes/no.

Given all this, and given that I'm making a judgment, I lean NO. Reasons:
1. Prop 42 is fundamentally a vehicle to nullify Prop 40 through a vote-counting mechanism that could block a majority-approved measure — anti-democratic.
2. It removes a revenue option in a state with fiscal needs.
3. Its "public benefit" (retirement protection) is speculative, and the measure was clearly funded to kill the billionaire tax.

However, I want to reconsider the economic case against wealth taxes, which is a legitimate consideration for a NO on 40 / YES on 42...

Actually, I keep going back and forth. Let me settle it with a clear principle:

My recommendation on Prop 42: **NO**.

Primary reasons:
- It is structurally designed to override the majority's will on Prop 40 (the billionaire tax). Even if Prop 40 passes with a majority, it could be invalidated if it receives fewer yes votes than Prop 42. Allowing a smaller, better-funded coalition to veto a majority-approved tax through a side measure is a democratic deficit.
- It reduces the state's fiscal flexibility at a time of significant unfunded obligations.
- The legitimate-sounding "retirement protection" rationale is, in this context, secondary; no retirement/savings tax is currently on the ballot or clearly imminent, so the measure's binding effect is really on the wealth tax.

I'm fairly confident in NO. But let me do a bit more research to confirm my understanding of the 40/42 interaction and the legal details, so my answer is well-grounded. Let me look at the legal text and some expert commentary.

**Prop 42 (Nov 3, 2026, CA):**
- An initiative constitutional amendment placed on the ballot by petition
- Prohibits new state taxes on the ownership of personal property (financial assets, retirement, savings)
- Limits/limits retroactive taxes (taxes based on the taxpayer's past conduct)
- Invalidates taxes enacted on or after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure
- Fiscal impact: taxes may not increase as much going forward

**Strategic interactions (per the LAO — the state's nonpartisan analyst):**
- If Prop 42 gets more "yes" votes than Prop 40 (the one-time 5% billionaire wealth tax), courts may find Prop 42 and Prop 40 conflict, in which case Prop 40 could be blocked from taking effect even if it passes.
- Prop 41 (restricts new state taxes that are excluded from spending caps) also interacts with Prop 40.

**Supporters:**
- Coalition of seniors, veterans, small business owners, blue-collar workers: California Professional Firefighters, State Building & Construction Trades Council, AMVETS, Peace Officers Research Association, California Senior Alliance
- Funded in part by Sergey Brin (per the opposition side, over $57 million)
- Total reported contributions: $127,977,037 for vs $22,741,302 against (as of Oct 22, 2026)

**Opponents:**
- Bernie Sanders, SEIU-UHW West, healthcare workers
- Argument: this is a billionaire-funded trick to undo Prop 40 (the billionaire tax); billionaires would rather see healthcare lose funding than pay taxes.

**Key analysis points:**
- Currently, there are no state taxes on the ownership of financial assets; CA taxes income from assets but not the ownership itself.
- The "double taxation" claim: income is taxed when earned, and taxing savings would be a second tax. This is a reasonable characterization — a tax on asset ownership would tax the same dollars that were already taxed as income (assuming no intervening consumption).
- Prop 42 would prohibit any new personal property tax by either the Legislature or ballot measure (per the argument language: "whether proposed by the legislature or by ballot measure").
- Retroactive tax restriction: taxes must apply only after voter approval / prospectively.

2. Prohibition of retroactive taxes — generally a sound principle of tax fairness.
3. Prevents "double taxation" of income that has already been taxed.
4. The protection applies to all Californians, not just the wealthy.

**Arguments in favor of NO:**
1. The main practical effect is to block Prop 40 (the billionaire tax) — if Prop 42 wins with more votes, Prop 40 is invalidated. In other words, a "yes" vote could take away healthcare funding that the majority voted for via Prop 40.
2. Reduces the state's future flexibility to raise revenue — in a state with large budget gaps and unfunded liabilities (pension obligations), this could constrain options.
3. It's a billionaire-funded measure (Brin) — the "retirement protection" framing may be a cover for undoing the billionaire tax.

But a state-level tax on vehicle ownership, or on the value of collectibles/fine art/jewelry, etc., would be blocked.
5. If you support Prop 40 (billionaire tax), then voting yes on Prop 42 is self-defeating: Prop 42 could nullify Prop 40.

- If you don't want the billionaire tax: vote YES on Prop 42 (and/or vote NO on 40).

content.text:
November 3, 2026 Ballot
Page 1 of 3
PROPOSITION 42
Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive
State Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
ANALYSIS OF MEASURE
BACKGROUND
Certain Personal Property Is Taxed in California. Both the state and local governments tax
the ownership of certain personal property. These taxes are based on the property’s value.
Personal property is all the things that people own other than real estate. One example of these
kinds of taxes is the vehicle license fee that car and truck owners pay to the Department of Motor
Vehicles each year. Another example is the property taxes owners of business equipment pay to
the county each year.
Ownership of Financial Assets Is Not Taxed. The ownership of many types of personal
property is not taxed. One major example is financial assets like stocks and investment accounts.
Although the state does tax income people make from their financial assets, there is no tax for
simply owning those assets.
PROPOSAL
Prohibits New Taxes on Financial Assets or Other Personal Property. Under
Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property would
not be allowed.
Limits Retroactive Taxes. Proposition 42 limits the situations that a ballot measure or the
Legislature can raise any tax retroactively. A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that
happened in the past. An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.
November 3, 2026 BallotSubject to court-ordered changes
Page 2 of 3
FISCAL EFFECTS
Possibility That Tax Revenues Will Be Lower in the Future. Proposition 42 restricts the
options the state has to raise taxes in the future. This could make it somewhat harder for the state
to raise taxes. This could reduce future tax revenues. When and by how much future revenues
would be reduced is unclear.
November 3, 2026 BallotSubject to court-ordered changes
Page 3 of 3
YES/NO STATEMENT
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership
of financial assets or other personal property.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish
new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST’S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT
• Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future.
BALLOT LABEL
Fiscal Impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future.

# Taxing wealth is a dangerous step toward taxing retirement savings
This November, Californians have an opportunity to protect the hard-earned retirement savings they have earned.
For the workers I represent, retirement isn’t a windfall.
It’s earned across jobsites from thousands of hours worked, over decades of early mornings, long shifts and hard physical work.
We need to protect what we’ve saved — and that’s why I’m voting yes on Proposition 42.
Working people already pay income taxes on the money they earn.
They shouldn’t pay taxes on that money twice simply because it’s sitting in a retirement or savings account.
Proposition 42 prevents that double taxation by closing a loophole in California’s Constitution that allows new taxes to be imposed on retirement accounts, life savings and other personal property.
...
Eighty-five percent of Californians say the cost of living or taxes are making it harder to save for retirement.
The last thing working families need is to worry that what they’ve managed to put away could be taxed again.
...
Proposition 42 backs that last promise.
It doesn’t take anything away from working families.
It makes sure what they’ve earned stays theirs.
You earned and saved it.
Proposition 42 would protect it.
...
### Insights
#### Ideas expressed in the piece

2. Your last-minute guide to all California propositions
https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-31/la-me-all-california-propositions-last-minute-voter-guide
# Your last-minute guide to all California propositions
## Proposition 42
Proposition 42 would limit the state’s ability to impose certain new taxes.
...
Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on “retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and other forms of personal savings” that take effect after Jan. 1, 2026.
It also would bar retroactive taxes on past earnings unless the state is using revenue from the tax to respond to emergencies such as a fire or a flood.
...
### The impact
The Legislative Analyst’s Office says Proposition 42 could nullify Proposition 40 because the two measures conflict with each other.
If voters approve both, the one with the most “yes” votes generally would become law, the office says.
...
The measure states that its purpose is to protect Californians’ ability to save for retirement and the future, though opponents say it’s meant to trick voters into canceling the billionaire tax.
“Taxes and cost of living are already too high in California — we need protection against taxes on our personal property and retirement savings,” supporters wrote in favor of the measure.
...
“Don’t be fooled — Prop.
42 is not really about protecting your retirement savings from new taxes,” SEIU-UHW Chief of Staff Suzanne Jimenez wrote in arguments against the proposition.
“It’s a redundant, expensive trick to allow approximately 200 billionaires to keep avoiding paying their own taxes.”

3. Should California tax billionaires? How McClatchy Editorial Board sees Props. 40, 41 & 42
https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317789904.html
Prop.
42 is pitched as a safeguard for personal property and 401(k) accounts, barring new state taxes on those assets and restricting certain retroactive taxes.
The editorial board describes it bluntly as a poison pill.
The suggestion that any governor would raid middle-class retirement accounts, the board writes, is implausible — any governor who tried “would soon be unemployed.”
Even the Legislature, which the board characterizes as inclined to spend more than it should, “knows not to mess with your 401(k).”
Opponents also note it appears to be an unsettled legal question whether retirement accounts can be taxed at all, because no government has tried.
Prop.
42 would embed its restrictions in the California Constitution, leaving voters as the only route to change them.
The board argues it would create “the illusion of permanently settling California tax policy on financial assets and other personal property” while in fact restricting the state’s future tax options — until the next constitutional amendment or competing voter-approved measure altered that policy.
The real function is familiar: if Prop.
42 collects more “yes” votes than Prop.
40, the wealth tax does not take effect.
“Prop.

I've got a solid grasp of the core details now. Key facts so far:

**Prop 42 (Nov 3, 2026, CA):**
- An initiative constitutional amendment placed on the ballot by petition
- Prohibits new state taxes on the ownership of personal property (financial assets, retirement, savings)
- Limits/limits retroactive taxes (taxes based on the taxpayer's past conduct)
- Invalidates taxes enacted on or after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure
- Fiscal impact: taxes may not increase as much going forward

**Strategic interactions (per the LAO — the state's nonpartisan analyst):**
- If Prop 42 gets more "yes" votes than Prop 40 (the one-time 5% billionaire wealth tax), courts may find Prop 42 and Prop 40 conflict, in which case Prop 40 could be blocked from taking effect even if it passes.
- Prop 41 (restricts new state taxes that are excluded from spending caps) also interacts with Prop 40.

**Supporters:**
- Coalition of seniors, veterans, small business owners, blue-collar workers: California Professional Firefighters, State Building & Construction Trades Council, AMVETS, Peace Officers Research Association, California Senior Alliance
- Funded in part by Sergey Brin (per the opposition side, over $57 million)
- Total reported contributions: $127,977,037 for vs $22,741,302 against (as of Oct 22, 2026)

**Opponents:**
- Bernie Sanders, SEIU-UHW West, healthcare workers
- Argument: this is a billionaire-funded trick to undo Prop 40 (the billionaire tax); billionaires would rather see healthcare lose funding than pay taxes.

**Key analysis points:**
- Currently, there are no state taxes on the ownership of financial assets; CA taxes income from assets but not the ownership itself.
- The "double taxation" claim: income is taxed when earned, and taxing savings would be a second tax. This is a reasonable characterization — a tax on asset ownership would tax the same dollars that were already taxed as income (assuming no intervening consumption).
- Prop 42 would prohibit any new personal property tax by either the Legislature or ballot measure (per the argument language: "whether proposed by the legislature or by ballot measure").
- Retroactive tax restriction: taxes must apply only after voter approval / prospectively.

Let me consider the analysis:

**Arguments in favor of YES:**
1. Constitutional protection of personal property (retirement accounts, savings, 401(k)s, IRAs, pensions) from future taxes. Currently, there are no such taxes, so this is forward-looking protection.
2. Prohibition of retroactive taxes — generally a sound principle of tax fairness.
3. Prevents "double taxation" of income that has already been taxed.
4. The protection applies to all Californians, not just the wealthy.

**Arguments in favor of NO:**
1. The main practical effect is to block Prop 40 (the billionaire tax) — if Prop 42 wins with more votes, Prop 40 is invalidated. In other words, a "yes" vote could take away healthcare funding that the majority voted for via Prop 40.
2. Reduces the state's future flexibility to raise revenue — in a state with large budget gaps and unfunded liabilities (pension obligations), this could constrain options.
3. It's a billionaire-funded measure (Brin) — the "retirement protection" framing may be a cover for undoing the billionaire tax.
4. "Personal property" is a broad term — could it also block future taxes on vehicles, business equipment, etc.? But a state-level tax on vehicle ownership, or on the value of collectibles/fine art/jewelry, etc., would be blocked.
5. If you support Prop 40 (billionaire tax), then voting yes on Prop 42 is self-defeating: Prop 42 could nullify Prop 40.

- If you want Prop 40 to pass and be in effect: vote NO on Prop 42 (and YES on 40).
- If you don't want the billionaire tax: vote YES on Prop 42 (and/or vote NO on 40).

I've researched this thoroughly across the official Voter Information Guide, the Legislative Analyst's Office analysis, campaign arguments/rebuttals, and independent reporting (LA Times, McClatchy, SF Chronicle, CalMatters, Politico, CBS) plus tax-law commentary.

## **NO**

Here's why, in brief:

**1. Its real, binding effect is a "poison pill" against the billionaire tax (Prop 40).** Prop 42's core legal function is to nullify Prop 40 (the one-time 5% tax on California billionaires) if Prop 42 gets *more "yes" votes than Prop 40* — even if Prop 40 itself wins a majority. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst's Office explicitly warns of this. The cleanest way to decide is to recognize that a "yes" on 42 is mainly a vote to kill the billionaire tax via a side measure.

**2. The "protect your retirement" framing is widely viewed as a decoy.** Multiple experts (including UC Berkeley law professor Brian Galle, who helped draft Prop 40) and editorial boards describe the retirement-savings warnings as a "red herring." California does not currently tax the ownership of financial assets, and no retirement/savings tax is actually pending — so the stated purpose doesn't match the measure's timing, funding (~$128M, largely from billionaire donors like Sergey Brin), or structure.

**3. It imposes a permanent constitutional tax restriction on speculative grounds.** It would lock the state into its Constitution against *any* new personal-property tax, reducing fiscal flexibility in a state with large unfunded pension liabilities and volatile revenues — all to preempt a tax that isn't on the ballot for ordinary people.

**4. It's structurally anti-democratic.** It lets a smaller, heavily funded coalition override the majority's direct decision on the actual tax question (Prop 40) through a "most yes votes wins" conflict rule. If you oppose the billionaire tax, the direct and honest way to say so is to vote **NO on Prop 40** — not to pass a separate constitutional amendment with a misleading label.

**Bottom line:** Vote **NO** on Prop 42. (If you support the billionaire tax, NO is even more clear-cut; if you oppose it, vote NO on Prop 40 directly rather than through this decoy.)

I've researched this thoroughly across the official Voter Information Guide, the Legislative Analyst's Office analysis, campaign arguments/rebuttals, and independent reporting (LA Times, McClatchy, SF Chronicle, CalMatters, Politico, CBS) plus tax-law commentary.

## **NO**

Here's why, in brief:

**1. Its real, binding effect is a "poison pill" against the billionaire tax (Prop 40).** Prop 42's core legal function is to nullify Prop 40 (the one-time 5% tax on California billionaires) if Prop 42 gets *more "yes" votes than Prop 40* — even if Prop 40 itself wins a majority. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst's Office explicitly warns of this. The cleanest way to decide is to recognize that a "yes" on 42 is mainly a vote to kill the billionaire tax via a side measure.

**2. The "protect your retirement" framing is widely viewed as a decoy.** Multiple experts (including UC Berkeley law professor Brian Galle, who helped draft Prop 40) and editorial boards describe the retirement-savings warnings as a "red herring." California does not currently tax the ownership of financial assets, and no retirement/savings tax is actually pending — so the stated purpose doesn't match the measure's timing, funding (~$128M, largely from billionaire donors like Sergey Brin), or structure.

**3. It imposes a permanent constitutional tax restriction on speculative grounds.** It would lock the state into its Constitution against *any* new personal-property tax, reducing fiscal flexibility in a state with large unfunded pension liabilities and volatile revenues — all to preempt a tax that isn't on the ballot for ordinary people.

**4. It's structurally anti-democratic.** It lets a smaller, heavily funded coalition override the majority's direct decision on the actual tax question (Prop 40) through a "most yes votes wins" conflict rule. If you oppose the billionaire tax, the direct and honest way to say so is to vote **NO on Prop 40** — not to pass a separate constitutional amendment with a misleading label.

**Bottom line:** Vote **NO** on Prop 42. (If you support the billionaire tax, NO is even more clear-cut; if you oppose it, vote NO on Prop 40 directly rather than through this decoy.)

PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayer’s past activities. Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future. Supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; State Building & Construction Trades Council of CA; AMVETS Department of CA Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES

NO

ARGUMENTS
PRO
California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax retirement and savings—even though you already paid taxes on that money when you earned it! CON

Proposition 42
Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Analysis of Measure
Background
Certain Personal Property Is Taxed in California. Both the state and local governments tax the ownership of certain personal property. These taxes are based on the property's value. Personal property is all the things that people own other than real estate. One example of these kinds of taxes is the vehicle license fee that car and truck owners pay to the Department of Motor Vehicles each year. Another example is the property taxes owners of business equipment pay to the county each year.
Ownership of Financial Assets Is Not Taxed. The ownership of many types of personal property is not taxed. One major example is financial assets like stocks and investment accounts. Although the state does tax income people make from their financial assets, there is no tax for simply owning those assets.
Proposal
Prohibits New Taxes on Financial Assets or Other Personal Property. Under Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property would not be allowed.
Limits Retroactive Taxes. Proposition 42 limits the situations that a ballot measure or the Legislature can raise any tax retroactively. A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that happened in the past. An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.
Potential Interactions With Other Propositions
If Proposition 42 receives more "yes" votes than Proposition 40 on this same ballot, then Proposition 40 could be stopped from becoming law even if it gets yes votes from a majority of voters. This is because the courts could find that Proposition 42 conflicts with Proposition 40.
Fiscal Effect
Possibility That Tax Revenues Will Be Lower in the Future. Proposition 42 restricts the options the state has to raise taxes in the future. This could make it somewhat harder for the state to raise taxes. This could reduce future tax revenues. When and by how much future revenues would be reduced is unclear.
Yes/No Statement
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.

PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 42
YES ON PROP. 42: PROTECT YOUR RETIREMENT AND LIFE SAVINGS FROM STATE TAXES
California is now the third most expensive state to retire in the nation. Every year, higher costs and taxes make it harder to save. An April 2026 survey found 73% of Californians know someone who has had to delay retirement for financial reasons.
CALIFORNIA CONSTITUTION CURRENTLY ALLOWS DOUBLE TAXATION
Yet, California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax the value of our personal property like retirement funds and savings accounts, even though residents already pay income tax on that money when they earn it. This means politicians can tax the same money twice: once when you earn it, and again when it is sitting in your retirement funds or savings accounts. That’s double taxation!
In the last few years alone, the Legislature and special interests have introduced six separate proposals that would tax retirement and savings accounts.
Taxes and cost of living are already too high in California-we need protections against taxes on our personal property and retirement savings.
PROP. 42 PROHIBITS TAXES ON RETIREMENT AND SAVINGS
Prop. 42 amends the state Constitution to protect Californians from this double taxation by special interests and politicians. Specifically, the measure:
• Prohibits new taxes on personal property, such as retirement funds, pensions and savings accounts; • Prohibits retroactive taxes; and • Prohibits all new taxes on retirement and savings this year and in the future.
PROP. 42 PROTECTS ALL FORMS OF RETIREMENT FUNDS AND SAVINGS FROM NEW TAXES
Roughly 80% of Californians report having some form of retirement fund or savings, including young workers just beginning to save; teachers, firefighters and police officers with pensions; and retirees who depend on their savings for financial security.
This measure protects all forms of personal property from new taxes, including 401ks, pensions, IRAs and personal savings.
“Prop. 42 protects Californians’ savings and retirement. Whether it’s a union member’s hard-earned pension or a small business owner’s IRA, new taxes on retirement shouldn’t stand between people and the security they’ve planned for.” -Chris Hannan, President, State Building and Construction Trades Council of California representing hundreds of thousands of union construction trades workers.
PROP. 42 PROHIBITS UNFAIR RETROACTIVE TAXES
The state should not be able to pass new taxes that apply retroactively to money that taxpayers earned in the past. Prop. 42 requires any new taxes to apply only after voters have approved them.
“It’s a question of fairness and common sense. People plan their retirement for years-they deserve stable, predictable rules that don’t change after years of saving and planning. Prop. 42 provides that certainty.” -Sean Morgan, licensed financial advisor
Prop. 42 is supported by a broad coalition of seniors, veterans, small business owners, blue-collar workers, retirees, including groups like the California Professional Firefighters and Disabled American Veterans, Dept. of California.
Californians are already struggling with high costs of living and high taxes. Many work their entire lives to achieve some measure of retirement security. It should be illegal for politicians and special interests to tax our retirement and savings.
You earned and saved it. Now we need to protect it. Please join us in voting Yes on 42. YesonProp42.org
Michael Hedges , President
California Small Business Association
Shelley Huff , Commander
AMVETS, Department of California
Jennifer Yoder , Board Member
California Senior Alliance
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 42
THIS IS ANOTHER BILLIONAIRE-FUNDED TRICK
Don’t be fooled-Prop. 42 is not really about protecting your retirement savings from new taxes.
It’s a redundant, expensive trick to allow approximately 200 billionaires to keep avoiding paying their own taxes while YOU get stuck with the bill.
PROP. 42 WOULD CANCEL OUT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
Prop. 42 is a billionaire-funded scheme designed specifically to undo the California Billionaire Tax, Prop. 40.
Prop. 42 was put on the ballot because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share. They’d rather millions of working people lose healthcare than pay a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
WHO’S BEHIND THIS? SOME OF DONALD TRUMP’S DONORS
The billionaires behind this don’t care about protecting your retirement savings. They’re protecting themselves. They’ve been getting out of paying their own taxes for years through loopholes and tax breaks.
This sham initiative was created to trick voters like you into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce. That’s why you must vote NO.
PROP. 40 WOULD ONLY TAX BILLIONAIRES’ $2 TRILLION IN WEALTH
The billionaires behind Prop. 42 have spread lies about the California Billionaire Tax (Prop. 40), trying to trick voters into thinking that their retirement and savings are at risk.
Don’t buy the fear-mongering. The California Billionaires Tax ONLY applies to billionaires. It’s about making billionaires finally pay their fair share so we’re not stuck with shuttered hospitals and skyrocketing healthcare costs.
Vote NO on Prop. 42.
Suzanne Jimenez , Chief of Staff
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 42
VOTE NO ON PROP. 42. This is a billionaire-funded initiative designed specifically to undo the California Billionaire Tax, Prop. 40.
PROP. 42 WOULD CANCEL OUT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
Prop. 42 was put on the ballot for one reason-because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share. This initiative was created to trick voters like you into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce. That’s why you must vote NO.
Don’t fall for the billionaires’ lies. Prop. 42 isn’t about preventing new taxes on personal property. It’s about preventing one specific tax that billionaires want to avoid, because they’d rather millions of working people lose healthcare than pay a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
PROP. 42 WAS FUNDED BY BILLIONAIRES WHO WANT YOU TO PAY MORE FOR HEALTHCARE
One of Prop. 42’s main funders is Google founder and Trump donor Sergey Brin, whose wealth has DOUBLED to nearly $300 billion since Trump’s election. Now he’s spent over $57 million to fund sham measures like Prop. 42 that attempt to cancel out a billionaire tax. U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders called this arrogant move by Brin “unacceptable.”
Donald Trump took money out of working peoples’ pockets and gave it to billionaires like Brin through massive tax breaks. Now, the billionaires backing Prop. 42 want YOU to pay more for your healthcare.
VOTE NO ON PROP. 42 IF YOU SUPPORT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
We have a chance to make billionaires pay their fair share to keep hospitals open and healthcare affordable for California’s working families. Vote NO on Prop. 42.

Prop. 42 is supported by hundreds of thousands of seniors, veterans, firefighters, blue-collar workers, public-safety officers and working families because it protects the retirement and savings of ALL Californians from new taxes. Who opposes 42? One organization that wants to tax retirement accounts.
WHY WE NEED PROP. 42
Sacramento politicians and special interests have repeatedly tried to pass taxes on retirement and personal savings accounts in recent years. They’ve relied on a loophole in California’s Constitution that allows government to tax our income when we earn it, and AGAIN when it is simply sitting in our savings and retirement accounts.
CALIFORNIA IS EXPENSIVE ENOUGH WITHOUT DOUBLE TAXATION
Prop. 42 prohibits this double taxation by PROHIBITING ALL NEW TAXES ON RETIREMENT AND SAVINGS ACCOUNTS and other personal property, whether proposed by legislation or ballot measure, including proposals on this year’s ballot and in the future.

WHO BENEFITS FROM PROP. 42
Prop. 42 protects the retirement and savings for all Californians-young workers just beginning to save; teachers, firefighters and police officers with pensions; retirees and veterans who depend on their savings for financial security.
You saved it. You deserve to keep it.
Prop. 42 asks a simple question: should California politicians have the power to tax your personal property, including retirement and savings accounts?

I've researched this thoroughly across the official Voter Information Guide, the Legislative Analyst's Office analysis, campaign arguments/rebuttals, and independent reporting (LA Times, McClatchy, SF Chronicle, CalMatters, Politico, CBS) plus tax-law commentary.

## **NO**

Here's why, in brief:

**1. Its real, binding effect is a "poison pill" against the billionaire tax (Prop 40).** Prop 42's core legal function is to nullify Prop 40 (the one-time 5% tax on California billionaires) if Prop 42 gets *more "yes" votes than Prop 40* — even if Prop 40 itself wins a majority. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst's Office explicitly warns of this. The cleanest way to decide is to recognize that a "yes" on 42 is mainly a vote to kill the billionaire tax via a side measure.

**2. The "protect your retirement" framing is widely viewed as a decoy.** Multiple experts (including UC Berkeley law professor Brian Galle, who helped draft Prop 40) and editorial boards describe the retirement-savings warnings as a "red herring." California does not currently tax the ownership of financial assets, and no retirement/savings tax is actually pending — so the stated purpose doesn't match the measure's timing, funding (~$128M, largely from billionaire donors like Sergey Brin), or structure.

**3. It imposes a permanent constitutional tax restriction on speculative grounds.** It would lock the state into its Constitution against *any* new personal-property tax, reducing fiscal flexibility in a state with large unfunded pension liabilities and volatile revenues — all to preempt a tax that isn't on the ballot for ordinary people.

**4. It's structurally anti-democratic.** It lets a smaller, heavily funded coalition override the majority's direct decision on the actual tax question (Prop 40) through a "most yes votes wins" conflict rule. If you oppose the billionaire tax, the direct and honest way to say so is to vote **NO on Prop 40** — not to pass a separate constitutional amendment with a misleading label.

**Bottom line:** Vote **NO** on Prop 42. (If you support the billionaire tax, NO is even more clear-cut; if you oppose it, vote NO on Prop 40 directly rather than through this decoy.)
